title: Conley v. Gibson (1957)
summary: The Court permitted railway employees’ claim against their union to proceed under a broadly stated notice-pleading approach.
notes:
Historical holding and language. The no-set-of-facts phrase is not the operative Twombly–Iqbal test.

The opinion's famous (and since retired) standard: "a complaint should not be dismissed for failure to state a claim unless it appears beyond doubt that the plaintiff can prove no set of facts in support of his claim which would entitle him to relief"; Bell Atlantic v. Twombly (2007) declared this 'no set of facts' language to have earned its retirement.

The union, Local 28 of the Brotherhood of Railway and Steamship Clerks, allegedly acquiesced in the Texas and New Orleans Railroad's May 1954 discharge of 45 Black employees who were then replaced by white workers, and ignored the members' repeated requests for help.

sections.Parties: Black railway employees sued representatives of their bargaining union for allegedly failing to protect their jobs without racial discrimination.
sections.Material Facts: The employees alleged that their jobs had been abolished while white employees received the work, and that the union failed to give them the representation it provided to white workers. Their claim concerned discriminatory representation by the union, rather than merely disagreement with an employer’s personnel decision.
sections.Procedural History: The district court dismissed on the ground that the National Railroad Adjustment Board had exclusive jurisdiction, and the Fifth Circuit affirmed. The Supreme Court (Black, J., unanimous) reversed, rejecting the Adjustment Board argument, the argument that the railroad was an indispensable party, and the argument that the complaint lacked specific facts.
sections.Issue: Did the employees’ allegations sufficiently state their claim under Rule 8?
sections.Holding: Yes. The allegations gave the defendants fair notice of the claim and the grounds on which it rested.
sections.Reasoning: The Court described pleading as a means of informing the opposing party and enabling a decision on the merits. Discovery and other pretrial procedures would develop and narrow the dispute. Its often-quoted statement that dismissal was improper unless no set of supporting facts could be proved expressed a highly permissive approach. That statement must be situated in the course’s chronology: Twombly later rejected it as a governing description of pleading sufficiency.

learning.why: The Court permitted railway employees’ claim against their union to proceed under a broadly stated notice-pleading approach.

topics.cp-notice-pleading: Conley associated Rule 8 with fair notice and the opportunity to develop a claim through later procedure.
topics.cp-pleading: Its permissive formulation became the focus of later disagreement in Twombly.
topics.cp-precedent: Twombly expressly retired Conley’s no-set-of-facts formulation.
topics.cp-plausibility: Twombly expressly retired Conley's 'no set of facts' formulation, so the two cases must be read together on any Rule 8 exam question.
topics.cp-frcp-8: The holding construes Rule 8(a)'s 'short and plain statement' requirement directly.
